propositions.text: The claimant seeks refugee protection under sections 96 and 97(1) of IRPA.
propositions.quote: XXXXX XXX (herein "the claimant"), seeks refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (IRPA).

paragraphs.summary: The claimant seeks refugee protection under sections 96 and 97(1) of IRPA.

propositions.text: The claimant's allegations are those included in his Personal Information Form (PIF).
propositions.quote: The allegations for the claimant were those included in his Personal Information Form2 (PIF).

paragraphs.summary: The claimant's allegations are those included in his Personal Information Form (PIF).

propositions.text: The claimant's sister was a member of an underground Christian house church in Fujian, China, and fled to the USA after government discovery in 2004.
propositions.quote: The claimant's sister was a member of an underground Christian house church in their home area in Fujian province of China. In XXXX, 2003 she convinced him to attend the church. He was only able to attend the church on an irregular basis because he was otherwise busy XXXX. However, in 2004 the government discovered the sister's church and she was forced to leave the area and go to the USA, where she successfully sought asylum protection.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant's sister was a member of an underground Christian house church in Fujian, China, and fled to the USA after government discovery in 2004.

propositions.text: After his sister left, the claimant did not attend church for some time due to being busy, PSB visits, and not knowing another church.
propositions.quote: After his sister left the area, the claimant did not attend any church for quite some time. Firstly, because he was usually XXXXXX, secondly, because the Public Security Bureau (PSB) often came to the family home to look for the sister, and, thirdly, because he did not know how to find another church.

paragraphs.summary: After his sister left, the claimant did not attend church for some time due to being busy, PSB visits, and not knowing another church.

propositions.text: In 2008, the claimant joined another underground church but was caught twice by PSB, detained, fined, and warned of serious consequences.
propositions.quote: Then in XXXX, 2008 the claimant was introduced to another underground church by his friend and started to attend. However, the claimant was caught by the PSB on XXXX, 2008 when he was on his way home after the church service. They released him the next day after he had signed a document promising not to practice illegal activities again. Nevertheless, he decided to continue attending the same church, but was again caught by the PSB on XXXX, 2008 when he was acting as a lookout for the church service. This time he was detained for fifteen days and was forced to pay a fine. When he was released he was warned that any further arrest would result in serious consequences.

paragraphs.summary: In 2008, the claimant joined another underground church but was caught twice by PSB, detained, fined, and warned of serious consequences.

propositions.text: The claimant's parents arranged for him to leave China; he arrived in Canada in 2008 and joined church services in Toronto.
propositions.quote: His parents were very afraid for him, so they made arrangements for him to leave China. He arrived in Canada on XXXXXX, 2008. Since arriving here he has joined in church services in the Toronto area.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant's parents arranged for him to leave China; he arrived in Canada in 2008 and joined church services in Toronto.

propositions.text: The claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
propositions.quote: I find that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

propositions.text: The claimant's identity as a Chinese citizen from Fujian is established by his evidence and identity documents including Resident Identity Card and Hukou.
propositions.quote: The claimant's identity as a citizen of China, and of Fujian province in particular, has been established by his evidence and by his identity documents, specifically, by the certified true copy of his Chinese Resident Identity Card (RIC), and Household Register or Hukou, as tendered into evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant's identity as a Chinese citizen from Fujian is established by his evidence and identity documents including Resident Identity Card and Hukou.

propositions.text: The claimant said he attended church irregularly in 2003-2004, about six or seven times, and avoided PSB by going to a neighbour's home.
propositions.quote: The claimant was asked how often he had attended church in 2003 and 2004. He said he had not gone very often, perhaps once a month for a total of six or seven times. Since he was not present when any members of that church were arrested he did not know any details. I asked him if the PSB had been looking for him as a result. He said that they did not come to look for him, but he had avoided them by going away to a neighbour's home.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant said he attended church irregularly in 2003-2004, about six or seven times, and avoided PSB by going to a neighbour's home.

propositions.text: After his sister left, the claimant continued private religious activity by reading the Bible and praying at home.
propositions.quote: After his sister left the area, the claimant said that he continued private religious activity by reading his Bible and praying at home.

paragraphs.summary: After his sister left, the claimant continued private religious activity by reading the Bible and praying at home.

propositions.text: In 2008, the claimant attended another house church weekly with about twelve persons, missing only if ill or busy.
propositions.quote: When he found another house church through a friend in XXXX, 2008, he was again able to attend with other underground house church Christians. There were about twelve persons in the congregation. The claimant attended almost weekly, over the months from XXXX to XXXX. He did not go if he was ill or was XXXX. He noted that his income from XXXX decreased between 2004 and 2008 because there are XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.

paragraphs.summary: In 2008, the claimant attended another house church weekly with about twelve persons, missing only if ill or busy.

propositions.text: In 2008, the claimant was stopped by police with two others after church, detained overnight, questioned, and released after signing a promise not to practice illegal activities.
propositions.quote: He said that in XXXX, 2008 he was stopped by the police patrol with two other Christians after they left the church service. The police searched his bag and found Bibles, so they suspected underground Christian membership. All three were detained overnight, questioned by the PSB, and then released after they signed documents promising not to practice further illegal activities.

paragraphs.summary: In 2008, the claimant was stopped by police with two others after church, detained overnight, questioned, and released after signing a promise not to practice illegal activities.

propositions.text: The claimant's explanation for amending his PIF about the location of his arrest is not reasonable or persuasive.
propositions.quote: I do not accept his explanation as reasonable. One is either at the service or not. The location of the arrest by PSB is an important point in the account. In my view the plain language of the original narrative is inconsistent with the revision, and he failed to adequately explain this.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant's explanation for amending his PIF about the location of his arrest is not reasonable or persuasive.

propositions.text: The claimant's failure to mention others arrested with him in his PIF is an important inconsistency without reasonable explanation.
propositions.quote: This is an important inconsistency for which he failed to give any reasonable explanation.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant's failure to mention others arrested with him in his PIF is an important inconsistency without reasonable explanation.

propositions.text: The claimant's handwritten declaration states he was arrested during the meeting, contradicting his later testimony about being arrested on the way home.
propositions.quote: The wording of this declaration is very clear. I do not understand why he would write down that the PSB arrested him during the meeting, if the more recent evidence he gave was that the arrests occurred when people had left and were making their way home.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant's handwritten declaration states he was arrested during the meeting, contradicting his later testimony about being arrested on the way home.

propositions.text: The claimant's inconsistencies about his arrest location and number arrested justify a negative credibility inference.
propositions.quote: I therefore draw a negative credibility inference as a result of all the foregoing concerns.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant's inconsistencies about his arrest location and number arrested justify a negative credibility inference.

propositions.text: Why did PSB not consider the sister's situation when interrogating the claimant in 2008?
propositions.quote: I was puzzled that if his sister had been forced to flee the area as a wanted person because of her underground church activity in 2004, which was a few years before the claimant's problems, and he was held overnight for further interrogation by the PSB, why the authorities did not consider his sister's situation in assessing that of the claimant.

paragraphs.summary: The court questions why PSB did not consider the sister's situation when interrogating the claimant in 2008.

propositions.text: It is not credible that PSB would ignore the sister's illegal religious activity when assessing the claimant's case.
propositions.quote: If his sister had indeed been discovered as being involved in an illegal religious organization in 2004, and forced to leave the country to make an asylum claim in the USA, I do not think it credible that the PSB would have ignored this in assessing the claimant's case.

paragraphs.summary: It is not credible that PSB would ignore the sister's illegal religious activity when assessing the claimant's case.

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, the PSB did not arrest the claimant or others on the alleged dates in 2008.
propositions.quote: I conclude, on the balance of probabilities, given these important and unexplained inconsistencies and implausibilities, that the PSB did not arrest him or any church attendees on XXXX XX or XX, 2008, as he has alleged.

paragraphs.summary: On balance of probabilities, the PSB did not arrest the claimant or others on the alleged dates in 2008.

propositions.text: The claimant's Declaration at arrival omitted mention of further church activities after initial detention, a significant omission.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, I note that his Declaration,7 which he wrote when he first arrived at Pearson International Airport in Toronto, made no mention that he was involved in any further church activities after the initial detention on XXXX, 2008.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant's Declaration at arrival omitted mention of further church activities after initial detention, a significant omission.

propositions.text: Claimant omitted mention of sister's underground church problems, drawing negative credibility inference.
propositions.quote: I draw another negative credibility inference from this important omission.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant omitted sister's underground church problems, drawing a negative credibility inference.

propositions.text: Claimant omitted post-detention church raid warning from narrative, explaining he wrote only simple reasons.
propositions.quote: Again I noted to him that this was not in his PIF narrative, and asked why not. He said that he only wrote simple reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant omitted post-detention church raid warning from narrative, claimant said he wrote only simple reasons.

propositions.text: Claimant omitted important information about similarly situated persons, drawing further negative credibility inference.
propositions.quote: Absent any reasonable explanation, I draw a further negative credibility inference.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant omitted important information about similarly situated persons, drawing further negative credibility inference.

propositions.text: Claimant omitted significant new information about re-arrest risk after PIF, drawing negative inference.
propositions.quote: I draw a negative inference.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant omitted significant new information about re-arrest risk after PIF, drawing negative inference.

propositions.text: No credible evidence that detentions or sentences occur in Fujian for mere church members or attendees.
propositions.quote: I have no credible or trustworthy evidence that such detentions or sentences occur in Fujian, and certainly not for mere church members or attendees.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no credible evidence that detentions or sentences occur in Fujian for mere church members or attendees.

propositions.text: Claimant could not recall number of PSB visits, drawing negative inference about intensity of interest.
propositions.quote: He could not even hazard an approximation, so I draw a negative inference.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant could not recall number of PSB visits, drawing negative inference about intensity of interest.

propositions.text: Claimant said PSB visited home multiple times since 2009; no arrest warrants or summons left with family.
propositions.quote: The claimant said that the PSB had been visiting his home to look for him a number of times since XXXX 2009...There has not been any arrest warrants/summons left with his family.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence states police commonly leave summons with family, though not proper procedure.
propositions.quote: ...it is very common in China for the police authorities to leave a summons or subpoena with family members...This is not actually the proper procedure, but it happens all the time...

paragraphs.summary: The court notes claimant said PSB visited home multiple times since 2009 with no arrest warrants left; documentary evidence states police commonly leave summons with family though improper.

propositions.text: Documentation highlights PSB rarely uses arrest warrants; Procuratorate issues warrants after investigation.
propositions.quote: Other documentation10 highlights that the PSB rarely uses arrest warrants. The Procuratorate will issue an arrest warrant after the PSB has investigated the case...

propositions.text: China often detains people not in accordance with law; some areas do not follow national laws.
propositions.quote: China is still far from complying with rule of law standards...some areas of China follow practices which do not conform with national laws and regulation.

propositions.text: Statutes on arrest warrants and summonses for Guangdong, Fujian, Liaoning not found in sources consulted.
propositions.quote: The Information Request above also noted that statues on arrest warrants and summonses specific to Guangdong, Fujian and Liaoning could not be found among the sources consulted...

paragraphs.summary: Documentary evidence shows PSB rarely uses arrest warrants; China often detains unlawfully; statutes on warrants in Fujian not found.

propositions.text: Reasonable to conclude authorities investigated and identified claimant for illegal religious activities.
propositions.quote: it is reasonable to conclude that the authorities have concluded some investigation which gives rise to them stating that he was identified as being involved in illegal religious activities.

propositions.text: Reasonable to expect arrest warrant or summons would have been left with family given ongoing inquiries and arrests.
propositions.quote: it is reasonable to expect, given the documentary evidence, that an arrest warrant or summons would have been left with the claimant's family.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it reasonable to conclude authorities investigated claimant and would have left arrest warrant or summons with family.

propositions.text: Panel determines on balance of probabilities that authorities did not come making inquiries regarding claimant.
propositions.quote: the panel determines, based on the balance of probabilities that the authorities did not come making inquiries regarding the claimant.

paragraphs.summary: The panel concludes on balance of probabilities that authorities did not inquire about claimant.

propositions.text: Insufficient credible evidence claimant was underground church member, detained, or sought by authorities; claimant not credible Christian.
propositions.quote: I conclude that I have insufficient credible or persuasive evidence to demonstrate that the claimant was ever a member of an underground house church in China or was ever detained or sought by the authorities...I find...he was not a genuine Christian in China, and that he was not a credible witness.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes claimant was not underground church member, detained, or sought, and is not credible Christian.

propositions.text: No weight given to documents from China due to ease of fraudulent documents in Fujian, especially among people smugglers.
propositions.quote: I also give no weight to any documents purporting to be from China given that the country documentation confirms the ease with which individuals may obtain fraudulent copies...

paragraphs.summary: The court gives no weight to documents from China due to common fraud in Fujian, especially among people smugglers.

propositions.text: No weight given to document about sister's U.S. asylum claim as it is poor quality photocopy, illegible, and unverifiable.
propositions.quote: I give no weight to the document purporting to be about the sister's U.S. asylum claim...it appears to be a very poor quality photocopy...virtually illegible.

paragraphs.summary: The court gives no weight to document about sister's U.S. asylum claim as poor quality and unverifiable.

propositions.text: Document about sister's claim tells nothing about basis; claimant had opportunity and counsel to provide better evidence but did not.
propositions.quote: In any event, it tells me nothing about the basis of the sister's claim...He has had benefit of advice from competent legal counsel throughout.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds document tells nothing about sister's claim basis; claimant had opportunity and counsel to provide better evidence but did not.

propositions.text: Panel does not believe claimant is genuine Christian and would not necessarily practice Christianity if returned to China.
propositions.quote: The panel does not believe, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is a genuine Christian and, therefore, accordingly the claimant would not necessarily practice Christianity should he return to China today.

paragraphs.summary: The panel does not believe claimant is genuine Christian and would not necessarily practice Christianity if returned to China.

propositions.text: Panel finds claimant participated in Christian activities in Toronto to substantiate manufactured refugee claim; little weight to church documents.
propositions.quote: the panel finds that the claimant participated in Christian activities in Toronto in order to substantiate a manufactured claim...the panel attaches little weight to the photographs and documents from the church.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds claimant participated in Christian activities in Toronto to support manufactured claim; little weight to church documents.

propositions.text: Panel determines claimant is not Christian, was not Christian in China, and is not sought by PSB in China.
propositions.quote: the panel makes a determination, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is not Christian, was not a Christian in China and is not being sought by the PSB in China.

paragraphs.summary: The panel determines claimant is not Christian, was not Christian in China, and is not sought by PSB.

propositions.text: Protestant worshippers number 20 million in official church and 50-70 million in non-state churches in China.
propositions.quote: Protestant worshippers number at least 20 million people in the official church and between 50 and 70 million in the non-state sanctioned churches.

propositions.text: SARA states family/friends holding home meetings need not register; police disrupt home meetings citing disturbance or 'evil religion'.
propositions.quote: The website of the State Administration for Religious Affairs (SARA) states that family and friends holding meetings at home...need not register...police and officials...disrupted home worship meetings claiming...belonged to an 'evil religion.'

propositions.text: House churches face more risks when membership grows, use facilities regularly, or link with unregistered groups or overseas coreligionists.
propositions.quote: House churches faced more risks when their membership grew, they arranged for regular use of facilities...or forged links with other unregistered groups or coreligionists overseas.

propositions.text: Members and leaders of unregistered Protestant groups face harassment, detention, fines, beatings, arrest, mistreatment, and torture.
propositions.quote: Members and leaders of unregistered Protestant groups in China continued to face harassment and harsh punishment, including detention, fines, beatings, confiscation of property, arrest, and mistreatment and torture in custody.

propositions.text: Arrests and harassment of peaceful Protestant activity occurred in at least 17 provinces, most in Henan, Xinjiang, Shandong, Hebei, Zhejiang.
propositions.quote: arrests for and harassment of peaceful Protestant religious activity occurred in at least 17 provinces and two municipalities, with the most incidents occurring in Henan, Xinjiang, Shandong, Hebei, and Zhejiang provinces.

paragraphs.summary: Documentary evidence shows millions of Protestant worshippers; home meetings disrupted; house churches face risks; harassment and arrests occur in many provinces.

propositions.text: No persuasive information that religious persecution occurs in Fujian for groups similar to claimant's.
propositions.quote: there is no persuasive information suggesting that religious persecution is occurring for groups that are similar to the claimant's.

propositions.text: China Aid Association (CAA) reports five main persecution targets: house church leaders, urban churches, forced worship cessation, severe punishment, tighter control of Three-Self Church.
propositions.quote: Their report identifies five main targets of persecution: House church leaders, house churches in urban areas, forcing churches to quit worship meetings, severe punishment...and tighter control of the Three-Self Church.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no persuasive info of persecution in Fujian for similar groups; CAA reports five main persecution targets.

propositions.text: CAA President states east coast provinces more open with fewer reported Christian incidents, but underreporting possible.
propositions.quote: The President of CAA has stated that east coast provinces are generally 'more open' with fewer incidents involving Christians reported to CAA.

propositions.text: CAA reports one church demolished in Pingtan, Fujian in 2006; no context on reason, denomination, or timing.
propositions.quote: The CAA reported that one church was demolished in Pingtan in Fujian in 2006. The article does not provide context as to the reason the church was destroyed...

propositions.text: Mr. Bob Fu states Fujian and Guangdong do not have religious freedom; persecution is constant and unpredictable.
propositions.quote: With specific reference to the provinces Fujian and Guangdong, it is absolutely incorrect to find that there is religious freedom in these provinces...the persecution may come and go and not be totally predictable, but it is always present.

paragraphs.summary: CAA President says east coast provinces more open but underreporting possible; one church demolished in Fujian; Bob Fu states Fujian and Guangdong lack religious freedom with constant persecution.

propositions.text: Religious persecution of Protestant house churches occurs in China but is not general in nature.
propositions.quote: What is clear to the panel is that in China, religious persecution of Protestant "house churches" does occur, however, it is not general in nature.

propositions.text: Factors to consider include links with the West, evangelization, membership growth, use of facilities, leadership, rural/urban location, and location within China.
propositions.quote: Such factors as whether there are close links with the West, evangelization, membership growth to become large-scale congregations, arrangements for regular use of facilities, whether an individual is a leader, rural or urban areas and location within China are all factors to consider.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds religious persecution of Protestant house churches occurs in China but is not general; various factors must be considered.

propositions.text: Persecution incidents are likely underreported due to censorship and incomplete information.
propositions.quote: The panel is mindful of the caveat that the number of persecution incidents is likely to be much higher because of censorship in communications26 and even considered the possibility that not all information is available to commentators.

propositions.text: There is significant evidence of persecution in remote areas, including arrests, fines, detentions, and confiscations.
propositions.quote: Considering all these factors, the panel concludes that since there is a significant amount of information detailing very specific examples from areas much more remote and difficult to access than Fujian, which includes not only egregious examples of persecution such as arrests but also other forms of persecution such as fines, short term detentions, confiscation of materials, etc,

propositions.text: It is reasonable to expect persuasive evidence of raids or persecution in Fujian if it occurred.
propositions.quote: that it is reasonable for the panel to expect to see persuasive evidence that groups such as the claimant's, which are small and not required to register, are being raided and individuals being jailed or facing other forms of persecution in Fujian province.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence persuades the panel that the claimant's unregistered house church was not raided and authorities are not investigating the claimant.
propositions.quote: The documentary evidence persuades the panel, based on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant's unregistered house church was not raided and further supports the determination that the authorities are not making inquiries with respect to the claimant.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds persecution likely underreported but no persuasive evidence of raids or persecution in Fujian; claimant's church was not raided.

propositions.text: Even if the claimant is Christian, the court does not accept it based on knowledge, attendance, or baptism documentation.
propositions.quote: With respect to the genuineness of the claimant's Christian faith, even if I were to accept that he is a Christian, - which I specifically do not, - based on any Christian knowledge, any church attendance, or any documentation27 which indicates that he has been baptized,

propositions.text: Most Christian groups not members of PRAs no longer operate in strict secrecy but carry out public activities.
propositions.quote: I would refer to documentation,28 which states: Most Christian groups, the majority of which are not members of the PRAs, no longer operated in strict secrecy. Instead, they carried out public activities, including convening seminars, publishing materials, renting space for offices and events, and disseminating information on the Internet.

paragraphs.summary: The court doubts claimant's Christianity but notes most non-PRA Christian groups operate publicly, not in secrecy.

propositions.text: Between 50 and 70 million belong to non-state sanctioned churches in China; evangelization occurs.
propositions.quote: In addition, previously referred to evidence indicates that between 50 and 70 million individuals belong to the non-state sanctioned churches in China. It is clear that evangelization occurs in China.

propositions.text: Given public activities and no persuasive evidence of persecution in Fujian, claimant can freely practice faith there.
propositions.quote: Given the foregoing evidence of huge numbers of Christian practitioners in the non-state sanctioned churches, documentation which indicates that most Christian groups no longer operated in strict secrecy and carried out public activities and no persuasive evidence that individuals who have evangelized in Fujian province have faced any sort of persecution, the panel determines, that the claimant can return to his home in Fujian province and practice his alleged faith freely and openly.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds many Christians practice openly in China and claimant can freely practice faith in Fujian without persecution.

propositions.text: A recent decision by Justice Russell supports this decision; Fujian's profile is similar to Guangdong's regarding underground churches.
propositions.quote: The panel is supported in this decision, by a recent decision by Mr. Justice Russell.29 While this decision concerns an alleged raid in Guangdong Province, the profile of Fujian province is virtually identical in terms of country document evidence concerning policies and actions in response to membership in underground Christian churches.

propositions.text: Justice Crampton in Nen Mei Lin found it reasonable to conclude persecution in Fujian would be documented if it occurred.
propositions.quote: Justice Crampton's decision in Nen Mei Lin, concerning Fujian province, in which the court stated that in the context of the significant detail in the documentation, regarding the dates and locations of arrests and other steps taken to discourage Christian activity in China, it was reasonable for the Board to conclude that, if persecution of members of underground churches occurred in Fujian province, it would have been documented.

propositions.text: Justice Lemieux in Jiang noted minimal constraints on religious practice in Fujian; people generally practice freely.
propositions.quote: Justice Lemieux in Jiang31 noted that the documentary evidence concerning Fujian province indicates there is a minimum of constraints on religious practice, and people generally practice their religion freely.

paragraphs.summary: The court relies on recent judicial decisions finding Fujian similar to Guangdong with minimal documented persecution of underground churches.

propositions.text: Claimant has not met burden to show serious possibility of persecution or risk of cruel treatment in China.
propositions.quote: On the basis of the totality of the evidence, and the cumulative findings, I find that the claimant has not satisfied his burden of establishing a serious possibility that he would be persecuted or that he would be personally subjected to a risk to his life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture, by any authority in the People's Republic of China.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes claimant failed to prove serious possibility of persecution or cruel treatment in China.

propositions.text: Claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor in need of protection; claim is rejected by Refugee Protection Division.
propositions.quote: I determine that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. Therefore, the Refugee Protection Division rejects his claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects claimant's refugee claim, finding he is neither a Convention refugee nor in need of protection.
